rv.q: “Kinney and his cast find memorable moments in Shepard’s darkly satirical play...Time has diminished some...shock value and the Signature’s production doesn’t dig deeply enough into the feeling the play seems to be after: It doesn’t pulse with the agony of stunted existence.
The laughs Lois got in that moment were bigger and truer than anything else in the production, all because the sheep wasn’t trying and was just, accidentally, in the moment.
The Tates’ fridge is almost always empty, and there’s a similar sense of vacancy to the direction and performances in the New Group’s lackluster production of this 1977. Sam Shepard play.

The intensity of Shepard’s writing—which segues dazzlingly from brutal to whimsical to extravagantly operatic—is matched in director Scott Elliott’s impressive staging in one of Signature’s smallest spaces.
The poison has been absorbed, and luckily for us, if not for them, it’s lost none of its potency.
Curse of the Starving Class remains an enticing family drama that will keep you up at night wondering if we can escape our own fates.
Kinney's production does capture well Shepard's characteristic oscillation between hyper-real physicality and archetypal elements in the plot and characters.

"It's easy to understand how 'Curse of the Starving Class' both jolted audiences and cemented Shepard's reputation as a playwright in its 1978 premiere at The Public Theater by showing us the warts-and-all underbelly of America and this not atypical American family.
But I’ve begun to think that this play might require meatier direction to keep the audience from leaving hungry.

"Terry Kinney begins his solid revival of the 1978. Sam Shepard drama with a jolting coup de theatre...But aside from the onstage appearance of an adorable, scene-stealing lamb, the rest of Kinney’s production never quite matches the shock of its opening moments...There’s not a great deal of subtlety here, either in the performances or in...
What’s ironic is that the real warning should have been to advise audience members that they’ll be bored to tears during the course of this miscast, indifferently staged, sluggish revival.
It's hard to see that through the self-defeating opulence of this revival.
Unexciting, emotionally uninvolving…Few moments find the right balance between Shepard's earthy realism and his poetic demands.
Kinney seems to have decided that the play Shepard wrote isn't sufficiently meaningful or effective, so he decided to exaggerate everything.
To breathe theatrical life into this wild clan—and Shepard’s scorching dialogue—demands a degree of intensity that Scott Elliot’s production just can’t provide.
The cast is excellent, fearlessly handling the text's demanding ricocheting between absurdity and intense – often ferociously violent – realism.

While The New Group’s production of Curse of the Starving Class has its moments of the darkest kind of humor, it is in essence a tragic look at a desperate nuclear family that is failed by society and, above all, has failed themselves and each other, as with the innocent sheep.
The part that matters here is that we (meaning me) ended up not caring about any of these people.

cn.t: A mixed revival that struggles to balance Shepard's tonal shifts, with critics divided on Kinney's stylized direction and the cast's performances. Some praise its timely themes and intensity, while others find it emotionally uninvolving and overly opulent.
